messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tailor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame Osei sat in the tailor shop he had built from nothing, his hands steady on a bolt of charcoal wool, his eyes fixed on the door. It was a habit he could no longer suppress—every time the bell jingled, he mapped the distance to the exit, noted the angle of the counter, calculated whether he could slip past a customer if he needed to. Three years had passed since the bombing, but his body still behaved as though the next explosion was seconds away.

The attack had happened on a Tuesday, during the evening rush at the downtown transit hub. Kwame had been on his way home after delivering a custom suit to a client. He remembered the crush of commuters, the stale heat underground, the flickering fluorescent lights. Then the world folded into a roar that seemed to come from inside his skull. He remembered nothing of the next several minutes—only waking on the platform floor, ears ringing, a gash on his forearm, people screaming and running. The police later told him a man had detonated a vest. Kwame’s memory held only fragments: a blurred image of a woman’s shoe lying alone, the smell of burnt metal, the strange whiteness of the smoke. The gaps unsettled him more than the images that did come, because he could never be sure what he had seen and what his mind had invented.

In the months afterward, Kwame found he could recall the event with almost photographic clarity—but only when he did not want to. The film would start without warning: the pressure wave, the shatter of glass, the woman’s shoe. Other times, he could describe the whole thing to a friend or a therapist (he saw one briefly) and feel nothing, as though he were reciting a story about someone else. That numbness frightened him more than the fear did. If he could feel nothing about something so terrible, what kind of person was he?

That question became a shadow that followed him everywhere. He had always thought of himself as capable, as someone others could rely on. But after the bombing, doubt crept into every decision. Could he trust his own instincts? He had frozen during the attack—stood there, stunned, while others ran—and he had turned that moment over in his mind a thousand times. A strong person would have helped someone, would have done something. Instead, he had been useless. He became certain that he was weak, and that everyone who knew what had happened must see it too. He stopped going to the neighborhood gatherings he had once enjoyed. He stopped returning calls from his cousins. The feeling that he no longer belonged anywhere settled into his chest like a permanent cold.

At work, he made his shop a fortress. He moved his cutting table so his back faced the wall and he could see the entire room. He kept the door slightly ajar so he could hear the street. Whenever a customer walked in, he scanned them from head to toe, looking for anything unusual—a bulky coat, a nervous hand. He began picking arguments with clients over small mistakes in their orders, or with the delivery driver who was five minutes late. The fights made his heart race, but they also pushed away the intrusive images for an hour or two. The relief never lasted, and afterward he felt even more alone.

His evenings became a blur of phone games and streaming videos, hours lost in scrolling because stillness meant thinking. He could not make plans for the future—not for a vacation, not for the next weekend, not even for a dentist appointment. Every time he tried, a voice inside him whispered that there was no point, that something would happen to upend it anyway. So he lived day to day, drifting through his work, avoiding the weight of tomorrow.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a moment of quiet terror. He had been sitting in his shop after closing, phone in hand, when he realized he had spent four hours doing nothing—not even scrolling, just staring at the screen, waiting for the next day to start. He had stopped making eye contact with his own reflection. He was afraid that if he kept going this way, he would shrink until he disappeared entirely. He did not know if therapy could fix the memory gaps or the hypervigilance or the certainty that he was worthless. But he knew he could not spend another year hiding behind a wall, waiting for the next explosion.
